content: The trials and associated costs of equipment, training for healthcare workers, session frequency, and potential negative impacts on equity were significant considerations. Four members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) disagreed with the decision to make a recommendation and instead suggested that no recommendation would be more appropriate. Annex 3 (C8) provides a detailed summary of the judgments made by the GDG for each Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) domain. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines assistive products as any external product, including devices, equipment, instruments, or software, that is specifically designed or generally available to maintain or improve an individual’s functioning and independence, thereby promoting well-being. These products are also used to prevent impairments and secondary health conditions. In the context of managing low back pain (LBP), lumbar braces, belts, and supports, as well as mobility assistive products, are commonly used in clinical practice. For the purposes of the guideline, assistive products were limited to external devices and equipment, excluding software products. Lumbar braces, belts, and supports can be either rigid (plastic) or non-rigid (elastic or non-elastic) and may include rigid inserts. These devices are designed to wrap around the lumbar or thoracolumbar trunk to restrict mobility, reduce strain, and decrease physical demands on the lower back. They are frequently used for chronic primary low back pain (CPLBP) as a treatment or to prevent pain recurrence. These products are widely accessible in most countries, though their use may be limited by cost (often an out-of-pocket expense) and climate (difficult to wear in high temperatures). Mobility assistive products, such as wheelchairs, mobility scooters, tricycles, crutches, walking sticks/canes, and walkers, primarily address mobility impairments but may also influence mechanical load on the lower back by supporting limb movements. Long-term use of assistive products, including lumbar braces and supports, may be associated with potential harms such as dependence, fear-avoidance of movement, and deconditioning of trunk musculature. The WHO guideline for non-surgical management of CPLBP in adults emphasizes the need for comprehensive service provision, including person-centered assessment, selection of appropriate products, fitting, and user training. Follow-up services should also be available for reassessment, maintenance, and repair of the products. The context of use should be considered to ensure the product is suitable for the individual’s environment. Mobility assistive products should always be provided by trained personnel, and WHO offers training in the safe and effective provision of these products through its Training in Assistive Products (TAP) program. WHO also provides specifications for various mobility assistive products, such as wheelchairs, pressure cushions, and walking aids, and has co-published a technical guide with UNICEF for countries on assistive product procurement. The evidence for the benefits and harms of lumbar braces, belts, and supports for CPLBP treatment was derived from seven trials (eight reports) involving 647 participants aged 25–78 years. No trials allowed data extraction for older adults (aged 60 years and above) separately. Four trials were conducted in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), while three were conducted in high-income countries (HICs). All trials compared lumbar supports to usual care, isolating the intervention’s effect. Meta-analyses included trials comparing lumbar supports with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) versus NSAIDs alone. Low-certainty evidence suggested that lumbar supports might reduce pain in the short term (four weeks), but this finding was not supported when considering additional trials with missing data. It remains uncertain whether lumbar supports make little to no difference in pain or disability outcomes at any time point due to very low certainty of evidence. No trials reported on harms. The GDG judged the overall net benefits of lumbar braces, belts, and supports to be trivial or uncertain for all adults, with one member suggesting moderate benefits based on clinical experience and indirect evidence. For older adults, the net benefits were judged to be uncertain due to the lack of evidence. Most available evidence was limited to short-term outcomes (four weeks), creating uncertainty about longer-term benefits. Harms were judged to be uncertain due to the absence of evidence, though some GDG members considered harms to be trivial based on clinical experience, while others highlighted potential harms with long-term use, such as dependence, fear-avoidance of trunk movement, and deconditioning of trunk musculature. The GDG judged the overall certainty of evidence to be very low, consistent with the systematic review team’s assessment. The balance of benefits to harms for lumbar braces, belts, and supports was largely uncertain, as none of the included trials reported on harms. Some GDG members expressed the opinion that the balance did not favor lumbar supports, while one member believed the balance probably favored the intervention based on indirect evidence from surgical populations. The GDG also noted variability in values and preferences among people with CPLBP, with some appreciating the security and identity offered by braces, particularly during acute pain exacerbations or return to work, while others found them stigmatizing and uncomfortable, especially in hot environments. The costs associated with lumbar supports were noted to vary widely, with high out-of-pocket costs in low-resource settings and negligible costs in settings where they are subsidized. Health equity could be reduced in some settings due to affordability and potential stigma associated with lumbar supports. The GDG judged that the provision of lumbar supports would likely be feasible in most settings due to their wide availability. However, acceptability could vary among people with CPLBP and healthcare workers. The GDG referred to qualitative evidence suggesting that some older adults use assistive products as part of their self-management approach, indicating probable acceptability among adults. The GDG reached a consensus to make a conditional recommendation against the use of lumbar braces, belts, and supports. This decision was based on the assessment of trivial benefits from meta-analyses, additional trials, and members’ opinions about potential harms with long-term use. The decision also considered the likely variability in values and preferences among people with CPLBP and the potential negative impact on equity in low-resource contexts. Five GDG members disagreed with this decision, suggesting that no recommendation would be more appropriate given the very limited certainty of evidence. The conditional recommendation against lumbar supports should not limit their use in populations with spinal deformities, as these represent a different clinical group. For mobility assistive products, the GDG noted the lack of evidence but emphasized the self-evident need for such products to support function and participation. The GDG provided a good practice statement with input from WHO’s Access to Assistive Technology Team.
